channel-f.subtitle: One console. A game you have not bought yet.
channel-f.summary: Jerry Lawson and his colleagues helped turn a television game into a platform: keep the machine, change the cartridge.
body: A new game once meant another machine. Dedicated home systems could offer variations on their built-in games, but their owners could not simply buy a new program and plug it in. Fairchild's Channel F, introduced in 1976, made that possibility a consumer product. The important object was small enough to hold in one hand: a cartridge containing a game's program.

Jerry Lawson led engineering work on the system. Fairchild had licensed an earlier design from Alpex, and bringing it into the living room required several kinds of expertise. Lawson's electronics work sat alongside Ron Smith's mechanical engineering and Nicholas Talesfore's industrial design. The cartridge and controller were physical objects that people would repeatedly insert, remove, grip and twist; a successful prototype also had to become something a household could use.

The result changed the relationship between a purchase and its future. A console could stay under the television while a library grew around it. New software could extend an existing machine's life, and publishers could sell games to people who already owned the hardware.

Lawson later founded Video Soft. His career joins engineering with entrepreneurship, and places a Black engineer near the centre of a formative consumer technology. Remembering the whole team makes that achievement more concrete: an influential idea became useful through the work of identifiable people, each solving part of the problem.

roberta-williams.subtitle: What if the room had a picture?
roberta-williams.summary: Roberta Williams took the places of a text adventure and made players look at them as well as read about them.
body: A text adventure asks a player to construct a place from sentences. Roberta Williams saw another possibility. In Mystery House, the player would still type commands and read responses, but a drawing would also show the location. A computer mystery could give its audience something to examine on the screen.

Williams designed the game and its story; Ken Williams built the software that brought it to the Apple II. Released through On-Line Systems in 1980, Mystery House used spare line drawings rather than the detailed paintings that later adventure games would make familiar. Those limits are visible, but so is the decision that mattered. Images became part of how a player understood a room, followed a mystery and imagined what might be waiting elsewhere.

Making the picture did not remove the need for language. Players still had to decide what an object meant and how to express an action. Looking and typing became connected activities. The drawing could establish a place immediately, while the words could explain what the drawing could not.

Williams continued exploring these relationships in games including King's Quest. As the hardware changed, the rooms became more elaborate and characters could move through them. The through-line is a designer choosing how to let someone enter a story. Before a graphical world could feel inhabited, somebody had to decide that an adventure should show its rooms.

dona-bailey.subtitle: A new way to move through the arcade
dona-bailey.summary: Dona Bailey brought programming experience from car electronics to Atari, then helped make a mushroom field feel immediate beneath a player's hand.
body: Dona Bailey was already programming microprocessors when she encountered Space Invaders. Her work at General Motors and the machines in an arcade were different products, but they shared a technical language she knew. In 1980 she moved into Atari's coin-operated games division. The question was no longer how to control a car's electronics; it was how to make a game that people wanted to play.

Centipede grew from a brief idea in Atari's notebook: a segmented insect descending onto the screen. Bailey worked with Ed Logg to turn that premise into the 1981 game. The centipede threaded through mushrooms, while other creatures disrupted the space around the player. The trackball made movement continuous and physical. A quick sweep of the hand could carry the shooter across the bottom of the screen.

Bailey wanted the game to look appealing in a dark arcade and its controls to feel approachable. The familiar insects, changing colours and direct movement gave it a character of its own. She has described hoping that everyone would enjoy it, rather than designing it only for a particular gender.

Her later interviews also describe the isolation of being the only woman software engineer in that division. Centipede's history includes both the pleasure of its control and the conditions under which it was made. Bailey's account restores a person, with specific skills and decisions, to a game that millions encountered without knowing her name.

carol-shaw.subtitle: A long flight inside four kilobytes
carol-shaw.summary: Carol Shaw needed more river than a cartridge could hold. She made the landscape from rules, then tuned those rules into a game.
body: The river keeps coming towards the player. Its banks narrow, obstacles interrupt the route, and the fuel gauge keeps falling. River Raid presents a long journey, but Carol Shaw had only a small cartridge in which to fit it. Storing a separate picture of every stretch of river was not an option.

For Activision's 1982 Atari 2600 game, Shaw used a repeatable number sequence to help decide the river's changing width. Short pieces of landscape could become a much longer course. Starting from the same value reproduced the same route, giving players a world they could learn rather than an arbitrary new river on every attempt.

The technical solution still needed a designer. Shaw adjusted how narrow the river could become and how often fuel appeared. Steering, shooting and refuelling pulled attention in different directions. A fuel depot could be an opportunity to survive longer, while a narrow channel punished an overcorrection. The landscape's apparent size mattered because it supported those decisions.

Her surviving papers preserve another side of the finished cartridge: code, working notes and design material. They let us follow the work behind the moving picture. A constraint became a method, and the method became something a player could feel as tension, rhythm and the possibility of making it a little farther upstream.

mule.subtitle: Your rivals are also your neighbours
mule.summary: Dani Bunten Berry and Ozark Softscape made competition depend on a colony that everybody needed to keep alive.
body: You can have money and still need something another player controls. That is the useful complication at the heart of M.U.L.E. On a small colony, players develop land and produce resources. They can compete for wealth, but their choices also shape the settlement that supports them all.

Dani Bunten Berry and the Ozark Softscape team released the game in 1983. Its production was collaborative: Bill Bunten shared design work and testing, Jim Rushing handled substantial calculation code, and Alan Watson worked on graphics and animation. In a contemporary interview, the team described beginning with the experiences they wanted players to have, before settling the theme and working out the program.

The auctions make that approach visible. A surplus is only valuable if someone will buy it; a shortage changes what a player is prepared to pay. Negotiation happens through movement and timing as well as calculation. People gathered around the same computer can watch a rival hesitate, hold out for a better deal or discover that their own plan depended on someone else's harvest.

M.U.L.E. makes the social encounter part of the machinery of the game. Its rules do not have to script every betrayal or act of cooperation. They create circumstances in which those moments can happen between people. Bunten's later interest in connected play followed that enduring problem: how can a computer help people make an interesting situation together?

tetris.subtitle: The gap you leave comes back to meet you
tetris.summary: Alexey Pajitnov gave a familiar kind of puzzle a moving deadline. The blocks kept falling, and a simple rule travelled around the world.
body: A good placement disappears. A bad one stays. Tetris makes the consequences of a decision unusually easy to see: complete a horizontal line and it clears; leave a hole and the pieces above it become tomorrow's problem. There is always another piece on the way.

Alexey Pajitnov developed the first version in Moscow on an Electronika 60. Inspired by the arrangement of pieces in a physical puzzle, he made a game of seven shapes, each built from four squares. The official chronology places its creation in 1984. What looks like a small set of possibilities becomes difficult because the player has to organise the pile while it is still growing.

The game spread through computer versions and then through a complicated international business of ports and licences. Its journey was carried by people negotiating across companies and borders, as well as by the appeal of the rules themselves. On Game Boy, a puzzle without a large fictional world could fit naturally into a portable machine and short stretches of time.

Watch the player's attention shift between the falling piece and the space waiting below it. That small movement contains much of the design: immediate action and longer planning happen together. Tetris travelled widely without needing every player to share a language, a character or an earlier gaming history. The problem was already there, visible in the gap.

game-boy.subtitle: The best screen was the one you could take
game-boy.summary: Nintendo made portable play a balance of battery life, size, controls and games. Game Boy's modest display was one part of that choice.
body: A handheld has to work after it leaves the demonstration table. It has to fit in a bag, run from batteries and remain useful away from the television. Nintendo's Game Boy, launched in Japan in 1989, answered those demands with a monochrome screen, familiar buttons and interchangeable game cartridges.

Gunpei Yokoi played a central role in Nintendo's portable hardware. Game Boy's design brings a practical question into view: which capabilities matter most in the place where the object will actually be used? The display was limited, but a player could carry the machine and a growing library together. Battery use and physical convenience were part of the experience, alongside the graphics.

Tetris suited that arrangement particularly well. Its shapes did not require a large screen to remain understandable, and a complete game could begin with very little explanation. Other designers found different uses for the same hardware. Nintendo's developers later recalled experimenting with a handheld Zelda until the apparently modest machine began to reveal more possibilities.

A console's future is also written by software that arrives much later. Pokémon reached the Japanese Game Boy in 1996, years after the original launch, and gave players new reasons to carry it and meet one another. The machine's history resists a simple race towards brighter displays: an older piece of hardware could become the setting for a new shared enthusiasm.

playstation.subtitle: Changing the material changed the possibilities
playstation.summary: Sony's first PlayStation joined real-time polygons to the capacity of a CD, giving developers new choices about what a console game could contain.
body: Open the lid and the change is easy to recognise. A PlayStation game sits on a compact disc, an object already familiar from recorded music. Sony launched the console in Japan on 3 December 1994; North America and Europe followed in September 1995. The format helped make room for more recorded sound, imagery and video, alongside the worlds being drawn in real time.

That capacity was a practical decision for developers as well as a selling point for players. Sony's history of the machine emphasises that CDs could hold more data than cartridge alternatives and could be manufactured more quickly and affordably. Games with large amounts of art and music, including Final Fantasy VII, could be built around those possibilities.

The new space did not dictate a single style. A racing game could make a circuit from polygons; an adventure could combine pre-rendered scenes with moving characters; a dramatic sequence could use recorded video. Designers had to decide where each technique helped the experience. More capacity created choices rather than automatically creating a better game.

The objects around the console also tell the story. A memory card held progress that could leave the machine, and the same disc drive could play an audio CD. PlayStation connected gaming with a wider household culture of music, screens and collected media. Its significance lies in the range of experiences that teams built from that combination.

doom.subtitle: The game continued after the download
doom.summary: id Software made a fast, forceful first-person game. Players gave it further lives by sharing it, competing in it and rebuilding its spaces.
body: A corridor is more than a picture in DOOM. It is somewhere to move quickly, a place that might conceal an opponent, and a route whose shape can decide a fight. Released by id Software in 1993, the game made speed, space and immediate response central to its first-person view.

Its developers combined programming, level design, art and sound into a recognisable rhythm. A player learns to read an opening, move through danger and keep track of what is happening beyond the edge of the screen. The space can feel threatening even when it is temporarily empty, because the player has learnt what might arrive next.

DOOM also had a way to reach people beyond a shop shelf. Its first episode circulated as shareware. A copy could be passed on, giving another player a substantial introduction before they decided whether to buy the rest. Distribution became part of the game's social life: someone who already had it could become the person who introduced it to someone else.

Network play and user-made levels opened further paths. Players could become opponents, map makers and organisers, extending the reasons to return long after an original level had become familiar. The development team supplied the foundations, while a community found new uses for them. To understand DOOM's longevity, follow both the game on the screen and the files moving between people's computers.

journey.subtitle: A person appears, without an introduction
journey.summary: Journey reduced the ways strangers could communicate, then made the decision to stay together feel unusually significant.
body: Someone else crosses the sand. There is no spoken introduction and no familiar player label above the figure. In Journey, meeting another person is first a matter of noticing how they move. A brief musical call can acknowledge them; continuing in the same direction can become a choice to travel together.

Jenova Chen and the thatgamecompany team built the 2012 PlayStation 3 game around an emotional journey towards a distant mountain. The landscape, animation and Austin Wintory's score give the passage its changing character. A wide desert and a difficult climb offer different settings for the same small figure, and for the companion who may be beside it.

The restricted communication changes what counts as an expressive action. Waiting is visible. Moving back towards someone is visible. A player cannot easily explain an intention in words, so the intention has to become something the other person can observe. Two strangers may read the same moment differently, which gives the encounter both uncertainty and possibility.

Journey's multiplayer design makes a small social act important without attaching a conventional conversation to it. The other figure is another person making decisions, rather than a character whose behaviour has been entirely written in advance. The mountain provides a destination, but the relationship can become the part a player carries away. A shared pace, a return, or a moment of help can give the passage meaning.

dandara.subtitle: Remove walking. Discover another world.
dandara.summary: Long Hat House began with the problem of fast action on a touchscreen. Dandara's unusual movement grew from taking that surface seriously.
body: Dandara cannot simply walk to the other side of a room. She moves by aiming and leaping between surfaces. A wall can become the next place to stand, and a familiar-looking platform room becomes a network of possible jumps. The movement rule changes how the whole world has to be read.

João Brant and Lucas Mattos, the founders of Brazil's Long Hat House, began the project with touchscreens in mind. They wanted action and exploration that felt native to touching and releasing a screen, rather than a console control scheme placed on glass. Limited access to console publishing helped direct that early choice. Raw Fury later joined as publisher, and adapting the idea to gamepads became another design problem rather than an automatic port.

The team also reconsidered whose story the game should evoke. A generic soldier gave way to a heroine inspired by Dandara dos Palmares and by ideas of resistance in Brazilian history. The developers have been explicit that the game's Dandara is fictional: this is a cultural reference, not a reconstruction of a documented life.

The 2018 release connects those decisions. An unfamiliar way of moving makes room for an unfamiliar world, while references closer to the creators' own culture give that world a particular identity. The history here is a small team choosing what to keep, what to change and how to reach players on more than one kind of device.

raji.subtitle: Keeping the story alive long enough to make it
raji.summary: For the team behind Raji, building a game rooted in Indian visual traditions also meant finding a way to sustain a small studio.
body: An ambitious visual world still needs a team that can afford to finish it. In Pune, Nodding Heads Games began developing Raji: An Ancient Epic with Indian and Balinese mythology and architecture among its references. Co-founders Shruti Ghosh, Avichal Singh and Ian Maude wanted to bring that setting to an international audience.

The route was difficult. A crowdfunding campaign failed, and continuing the project required personal sacrifices. An Unreal Dev Grant helped the studio survive until it secured a publisher. The finished 2020 game is therefore also the record of a production that had to change its plans and keep finding the resources to continue.

The creative decisions were specific. Research in Rajasthan informed the environments, while the heroine's background as an acrobat helped the team rethink movement and combat. Walls and pillars could become active parts of a fight rather than scenery behind it. A visual tradition had to become a place that worked under a player's control.

Raji belongs within a much broader history of game making in India, not at an invented starting point for it. Its story makes the practical work visible: choosing references, testing movement, reducing a plan to something achievable and finding the money to finish. The resulting adventure offers players a particular team's interpretation of those influences, carried into a game that could travel beyond the place where it was made.
